adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Removing the multiple-provider hard error while Default, FIPS1402 and Elytron all return order 200 means a tie is silently broken by ServiceLoader/classpath order (logged only at debug), so a FIPS deployment with crypto-default accidentally on the classpath can fail open to the non-FIPS provider.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` to no longer hard-fail when multiple `CryptoProvider`s are present. It now sorts by `CryptoProvider::order` descending and returns the first provider, only logging the rest at debug (common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java). However, the diff also sets `order()` to `200` for `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider`, and `WildFlyElytronProvider` (three separate files), so the sort does not break ties. With equal order values, the chosen provider depends on `ServiceLoader` iteration/classpath order, meaning a FIPS environment that accidentally includes the default (non-FIPS) provider could silently select it instead of failing, which is a security/correctness regression compared to the previous hard error.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java:44 — order() is added as an abstract (non-default) SPI method, so any third-party CryptoProvider compiled against the old interface throws AbstractMethodError inside the detectProvider sort once a second provider (for example the new authz-client one) is on the classpath, which breaks CryptoIntegration.init entirely.

authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:42 — One default-size EC key is used for ES256, ES384 and ES512, and the test only checks that the provider's own decode, encode, decode round trip matches itself (it never calls Signature.verify or compares with a reference), so curve/length mismatches that truncate or pad r/s, or a symmetric encoder/decoder bug, still go green.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds ECDSAAlgorithmTest which generates a single default EC keypair via `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` and reuses it for ES256/ES384/ES512. The test then only checks `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` -> `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` -> `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` round-trip using the same provider methods, without any `Signature.verify` or comparison to a known-good encoder/decoder. Given `algorithm.getSignatureLength()` varies by ES* (and the key size may not), padding/truncation issues or symmetric bugs in both directions could still pass. This is a concrete weakness in the newly added test rather than a runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:103 — concatenatedRSToASN1DER never checks signature.length against signLength: trailing bytes on an attacker-supplied JWS signature are silently ignored (malleable signatures still verify), and a short signature throws an unchecked ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of an IOException.

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER(byte[] signature, int signLength), the code assumes the input array contains exactly signLength bytes (two halves of length signLength/2) but never checks it. It blindly does System.arraycopy(signature, 0, r, 1, len) and System.arraycopy(signature, len, s, 1, len): if signature is shorter than signLength this throws an unchecked ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, and if signature is longer, the extra trailing bytes are ignored (only the first signLength bytes are used), which is an input-validation/security correctness issue for signature handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/AuthzClient.java:95 — AuthzClient.create pins the JVM-global CryptoIntegration provider using the authz-client classloader; when only that loader sees the stub AuthzClientCryptoProvider (for example modular or split classloaders), whichever code initializes first wins, and later Keycloak code in the same JVM gets UnsupportedOperationException from PEM, cert, cipher and signature calls.

authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:151 — integerToBytes silently drops high-order bytes whenever the encoded integer is longer than qLength (not just a single 0x00 sign byte), so a key/algorithm curve mismatch or a negative INTEGER produces a corrupt signature instead of an error.

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.integerToBytes(BigInteger s, int qLength), when s.toByteArray().length > qLength it unconditionally truncates to the last qLength bytes (dropping the most-significant bytes) without validating that the dropped bytes are only the expected single leading 0x00 sign-padding byte for a positive INTEGER. Since ASN1Decoder.readInteger() uses new BigInteger(bytes) (signed), a negative INTEGER or an oversized INTEGER (not merely sign padding) would be silently coerced into a different value, producing a corrupted r/s component rather than throwing an error. This behavior is directly present in the added code and matches the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:72 — readInteger passes the indefinite-length marker (-1 from 0x80) straight to read(), causing a NegativeArraySizeException, and a zero-length INTEGER makes new BigInteger(byte[0]) throw NumberFormatException; both unchecked exceptions escape the declared IOException contract.

authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:57 — The DER decoder is not strict: readTagNumber ignores the class and constructed bits (so 0x10, 0xB0 and 0xA2 are accepted as SEQUENCE/INTEGER), readSequence stops once length drops to 0 or below without checking the exact length match, and trailing bytes after the sequence are ignored, so non-canonical DER is accepted.

adjudication.rationale: The finding matches the new ASN1Decoder implementation. `readTagNumber(int tag)` masks the tag with `0x1f` and never checks the class/constructed bits, so a tag like `0xB0` yields `tagNo == 0x10` and will be accepted by `readSequence()` as a SEQUENCE, and similarly non-UNIVERSAL tags with low bits `0x02` can be accepted as INTEGER in `readInteger()`. Also, `readSequence()` decrements `length` by `bytes.length` in a `while (length > 0)` loop; if an element over-consumes, `length` can go negative and the method still returns without error (no exact-length enforcement). Finally, `readSequence()` does not verify that the entire input is consumed (no check for trailing bytes after the sequence), so extra bytes are ignored by callers like `asn1derToConcatenatedRS(...)`.

common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Multiple providers used to fail fast, but now Default, FIPS1402 and Elytron all return 200, so the winner silently depends on ServiceLoader/classpath order (for example, a non-FIPS provider can be picked in a FIPS deployment).

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider to no longer fail when multiple CryptoProvider implementations are present; it sorts by CryptoProvider::order (descending) and then silently picks foundProviders.get(0), logging the rest. However, the diff also adds order() to the interface and sets DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all to return 200. With equal order values, the chosen provider depends on ServiceLoader discovery order/classpath order, which can vary and can select a non-FIPS provider even when the FIPS provider is on the classpath—previously this situation would throw.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` from throwing an `IllegalStateException` when multiple `CryptoProvider`s are found to instead sorting by `CryptoProvider::order` and selecting the first, while logging the remaining “Ignored crypto providers” only via `logger.debugf(...)`. This makes the previous hard-failure on multiple providers disappear, and if multiple providers are present unexpectedly (or have equal `order()`), the selection becomes silent unless debug logging is enabled. That’s an observable/configuration-safety concern grounded in the change, but not a strictly verifiable functional defect since the new `order()` mechanism appears intentional.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/AuthzClient.java:95 — AuthzClient.create now fixes the JVM-global crypto provider using AuthzClient's classloader; in split-classloader containers the stub AuthzClientCryptoProvider can win, and later init(appLoader) calls do nothing, so other Keycloak libraries get a provider that throws UnsupportedOperationException.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())` in `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` (AuthzClient.java). The authz-client module also introduces an SPI-registered `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` (META-INF/services/...) whose implementation throws `UnsupportedOperationException` for most `CryptoProvider` methods (only ECDSA conversion and a few basics are implemented). `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider(ClassLoader)` selects a provider via `ServiceLoader.load(..., classLoader)` and now returns the highest-`order()` provider rather than failing on multiple; if the passed classloader only sees authz-client’s SPI, this stub provider will be selected. Since `CryptoIntegration` is a static integration point, initializing it from authz-client’s classloader can cause other Keycloak code (loaded under the same `CryptoIntegration` class) to later observe this stub provider and hit `UnsupportedOperationException` when calling other crypto operations. This behavior is directly enabled by the new early init call plus the new stub provider registration.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:76 — Most SPI methods (getSignature, getPemUtils, getX509CertFactory, getKeyFactory, etc.) throw unchecked UnsupportedOperationException, but the CryptoProvider contract declares no optional operations, so callers of CryptoIntegration.getProvider() only fail when they call a method.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` implementing `org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider`, but most required SPI methods (`getSignature`, `getPemUtils`, `getX509CertFactory`, `getKeyFactory`, etc.) are implemented as `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.")`. Since `CryptoProvider` does not declare these operations as optional, selecting this provider via `CryptoIntegration` (now initialized in `AuthzClient.create(...)`) can lead to late runtime failures if any of those methods are called. The diff does not show an actual call path that triggers those methods, so it’s not a directly verifiable broken behavior, but it is a concrete, diff-grounded contract/architecture issue.

matched_golden_ids: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same bug: the method intended to return the BouncyCastle provider instead returns the default KeyStore/provider (e.g., SUN), violating its contract and potentially causing algorithm/provider lookup failures.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Default, Elytron, and FIPS providers all return order 200, so where the old code threw on multiple providers (e.g. default plus FIPS on the classpath), a tie now silently picks whichever ServiceLoader lists first and can select a non-FIPS provider

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider to no longer throw when multiple CryptoProvider implementations are present; it now sorts by CryptoProvider::order (descending) and returns the first provider, merely logging the rest (common/.../CryptoIntegration.java). In this same diff, DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all implement order() returning 200, so a tie results. With multiple 200-order providers on the classpath, selection becomes dependent on ServiceLoader iteration order (not guaranteed), which can silently choose a non-FIPS provider where previously it would fail fast by throwing on multiple providers. This is a real behavior/security regression grounded in the code shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:73 — A zero-length INTEGER (02 00) makes new BigInteger(new byte[0]) throw NumberFormatException instead of the declared IOException

adjudication.rationale: In newly added ASN1Decoder.readInteger(), it reads the INTEGER length and unconditionally does `new BigInteger(bytes)`. If the encoded INTEGER has length 0 (DER bytes `02 00`), `read(0)` returns an empty array and `new BigInteger(new byte[0])` throws `NumberFormatException` (unchecked), not the declared `IOException`. This is a real, diff-grounded correctness issue in the added decoder.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:81 — readLength returns the -1 sentinel for indefinite length, but readNext adds it to the header count without checking, so it reads a bogus element and misaligns the stream
matched_golden_ids: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same root problem: readLength can return -1 as an indefinite-length sentinel, and subsequent arithmetic/aggregation on that value (e.g., subtracting remaining bytes or adding to header/offset) is performed without guarding against -1, leading to incorrect length calculations and misaligned/incorrect decoding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:57 — readSequence never checks that the elements exactly fill the declared length (a negative remainder is accepted) and ignores the constructed bit and trailing bytes

adjudication.rationale: In new ASN1Decoder.readSequence(), the loop decrements the declared SEQUENCE length by each element’s total encoded length, but never validates that the final remainder is exactly 0. If an element’s encoded length exceeds the remaining declared length, the remainder becomes negative and the method still returns successfully (loop stops when length > 0 is false). Additionally, it only checks the tag number (tag & 0x1f == SEQUENCE) and does not require the SEQUENCE tag to have the constructed bit set (e.g., it would accept tag 0x10 as well as the correct 0x30). It also doesn’t check for unread trailing bytes after consuming the declared length. This is a real parsing correctness issue in the newly added decoder used for ECDSA signature conversion.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:114 — Dead statements: two ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) calls build encoders whose results are discarded, then the same encoders are rebuilt inline at lines 119-120.

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider#getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the two standalone calls `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` construct encoders, write into them, and then discard them without using their byte output. The actual returned DER sequence is built again inline via `writeDerSeq(ASN1Encoder.create().write(...), ASN1Encoder.create().write(...))`. This is redundant/dead code (wasted work) but does not change behavior since the discarded encoders have no side effects.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java:44 — Magic order values (100 in AuthzClientCryptoProvider, 200 hard-coded in Default/Elytron/FIPS providers) have no named constants and the SPI javadoc does not document the ranges or say what happens on a tie.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new SPI method `CryptoProvider.order()` (common/.../CryptoProvider.java) and changes provider selection to `sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())` (CryptoIntegration.detectProvider). Multiple implementations hard-code numeric priorities (`AuthzClientCryptoProvider` returns 100; Default/WildFlyElytron/FIPS providers all return 200) with no named constants/enums, and the SPI javadoc only states “higher number has preference” but does not define ranges or what happens on ties. Ties are possible per the diff (several providers return 200), and tie-breaking is not specified in code or docs, making provider selection ambiguous if more than one such provider is present.

adjudication_records.issue_text: crypto/default/src/main/java/org/keycloak/crypto/def/DefaultCryptoProvider.java:84 — Default, Elytron and FIPS providers all return the same order 200, so the old fail-fast "multiple providers" error is now silently resolved by ServiceLoader classpath order and only logged at debug level.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` to sort providers by `CryptoProvider::order` (descending) and then always pick the first, only logging other providers at debug level (no longer throwing when multiple are present). In the same diff, `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`, and `FIPS1402Provider` all implement `order()` returning `200`, so ties are not resolved by the new mechanism; selection will depend on the `ServiceLoader` encounter order for equal `order()` values, and the presence of multiple providers is no longer surfaced as an error.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java:44 — order() is added as an abstract interface method rather than a default method, so every out-of-tree CryptoProvider implementation breaks at compile time.
matched_golden_ids: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both point out that adding order() as an abstract method on CryptoProvider breaks backward compatibility by forcing all existing implementations to implement it (compile-time failure), which matches the expected concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:61 — getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JDK default KeyStore provider, which does not match the method name or the Elytron provider's convention of returning null when BC is absent.

adjudication.rationale: In the new class `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`, `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, i.e., the provider for the JDK default keystore type, not a BouncyCastle provider (and not `null` when BC is absent). Given the interface method is explicitly named/typed as returning the BouncyCastle provider (and other implementations return an actual BC provider or `null`), this is a concrete, diff-verifiable incorrect implementation that can mislead callers expecting a BC provider reference.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:76 — About 15 SPI methods throw UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet."), which reads like an IDE-generated TODO and doesn't explain that the authz-client provider intentionally supports only ECDSA and keystore operations.

adjudication.rationale: In the new `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` implementation, many required `CryptoProvider` SPI methods (e.g., `getAlgorithmProvider`, `getCertificateUtils`, `getPemUtils`, `getSignature`, etc.) explicitly throw `new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.")`. This is verifiable in the diff and the message indeed reads like an IDE-generated placeholder rather than documenting an intentional partial implementation for the authz-client. While not inherently a correctness bug based solely on this diff (it may be by design and/or not invoked), it is a concrete, diff-grounded maintainability/clarity concern and could lead to confusing runtime failures if those methods are ever called.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:151 — integerToBytes and the ECDSA RS/DER conversion re-implement logic that already exists in the BC/Elytron ECDSACryptoProvider implementations, with no shared helper.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does add new ECDSA RS<->ASN.1 DER conversion code in AuthzClientCryptoProvider (plus custom ASN1Encoder/ASN1Decoder and integerToBytes), but the finding’s key assertion—"logic that already exists in the BC/Elytron ECDSACryptoProvider implementations"—cannot be verified from this diff because those existing implementations are not shown here. From the diff alone we can’t confirm duplication versus reuse opportunities in other modules.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Encoder.java:46 — The public write(BigInteger), which encodes an ASN.1 INTEGER, overloads the package-private raw write(int)/write(byte[]) byte writers, so the name is ambiguous; writeInteger would be clearer.

adjudication.rationale: In ASN1Encoder, method overloading between write(BigInteger), write(int), and write(byte[]) is valid and not ambiguous in Java; calls resolve by argument type. The finding is purely a naming/style preference (“writeInteger would be clearer”), not a verifiable defect or substantive review issue grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:66 — logger.debugf gets a pre-built non-format string (so any '%' in a class name would be misparsed), the loop leaves a trailing ", ", and the StringBuilder is built even when debug logging is off.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, the `StringBuilder` is only appended with Java class names plus ", ", so the claim that a '%' in a class name could be misparsed by `logger.debugf(builder.toString())` is not realistic/grounded (Java identifiers/class names cannot contain '%'). The other points (trailing ", " and building the StringBuilder without an explicit debug-enabled guard) are minor logging/perf/style nits and don’t constitute a verifiable defect introduced by the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Default, Elytron and FIPS providers all return order 200, so replacing the multiple-provider fail-fast with a sort silently picks an arbitrary tied provider (e.g. non-FIPS over FIPS) and logs the ignored ones only at debug

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider to sort providers by CryptoProvider::order (descending) and return the first, no longer failing when multiple providers are present. In the same diff, DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all implement order() returning 200, so the sort does not break ties. With multiple providers on the classpath, the chosen provider can therefore depend on ServiceLoader iteration order (not guaranteed by the diff), meaning selection can be effectively arbitrary. This is a behavioral change from deterministic fail-fast to potentially selecting an unintended provider (including non-FIPS vs FIPS), while only logging ignored providers at debug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java:44 — New abstract order() has no default, so existing third-party CryptoProvider implementations hit AbstractMethodError during the detectProvider sort and CryptoIntegration.init fails

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new abstract method `int order()` to the public `CryptoProvider` interface (common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java) with no default implementation. At the same time, `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` now unconditionally calls `CryptoProvider::order` while sorting providers loaded via `ServiceLoader` (common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java). In Java, any existing `CryptoProvider` implementation compiled against the previous interface (without `order()`) will not have this method and will throw `AbstractMethodError` when `order()` is invoked, causing `CryptoIntegration.init`/provider detection to fail at runtime. This is a real binary compatibility break introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/AuthzClient.java:95 — CryptoIntegration.init is first-caller-wins JVM-wide, so if AuthzClient.create runs first under a classloader that only sees AuthzClientCryptoProvider, the stub provider becomes global and later init(otherLoader) calls do nothing, which makes unrelated code hit UnsupportedOperationException

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())` in `AuthzClient.create(...)`, which can eagerly initialize the globally selected `CryptoProvider` based on the authz-client’s classloader. The authz-client also adds a `ServiceLoader` provider (`META-INF/services/...CryptoProvider`) whose implementation (`AuthzClientCryptoProvider`) throws `UnsupportedOperationException` for most `CryptoProvider` methods, so selecting it as the global provider could impact other codepaths that later rely on full crypto functionality. However, the claim that `CryptoIntegration.init` is strictly “first-caller-wins” and that later `init(otherLoader)` calls are no-ops is not shown in this diff (the `init` method behavior isn’t included), so the failure mode is a plausible architecture risk but not fully verifiable as a concrete defect from the provided changes alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:218 — getSignature/getKeyFactory/getKeyPairGen/getX509CertFactory/getPemUtils/wrapFactoryForTruststore throw an unchecked UnsupportedOperationException when simple JDK-backed versions exist, getting around callers that only handle GeneralSecurityException

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` registered via `META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider`. In that class, multiple required `CryptoProvider` methods (`getKeyPairGen`, `getKeyFactory`, `getX509CertFactory`, `getPemUtils`, `getSignature`, `wrapFactoryForTruststore`, etc.) currently throw unchecked `UnsupportedOperationException` (see the new file). While this may be acceptable if authz-client only needs the ECDSA conversion helper, it is a concrete, diff-grounded incompleteness/risk: if this provider ends up being the selected provider (e.g., in a minimal/classpath scenario), any code path calling those methods will fail at runtime. The finding’s claim about “callers that only handle GeneralSecurityException” is speculative, but the unchecked UOE behavior and the existence of simple JDK-backed alternatives is a valid review concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:134 — readLength returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding, which readInteger passes to read(-1), so the decoder throws NegativeArraySizeException (line 170) instead of IOException

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added ASN1Decoder, readLength() explicitly returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding (length == 0x80). Both readInteger() and readNext() then pass that length into read(length), which allocates `new byte[length]` (read():156-170). If length is -1 this triggers a NegativeArraySizeException instead of an IOException, matching the finding. The diff shows no guard against -1 in these callers.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:73 — A zero-length INTEGER makes new BigInteger(new byte[0]) throw NumberFormatException instead of IOException

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `ASN1Decoder.readInteger()`, it reads the INTEGER length and directly does `return new BigInteger(bytes);` after `byte[] bytes = read(length);`. If the ASN.1 INTEGER has a zero length (`length == 0`), `read(0)` returns `new byte[0]`, and `new BigInteger(new byte[0])` throws a `NumberFormatException` (runtime) rather than the declared/expected `IOException` for malformed ASN.1 input. There is no guard converting this case into an `IOException`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:57 — readSequence never checks that element sizes add up exactly to the declared length and ignores trailing bytes, and short-form lengths skip the bounds check, so malformed DER is accepted

adjudication.rationale: In ASN1Decoder.readSequence(), the loop `while (length > 0) { ... length = length - bytes.length; }` never validates that the consumed element lengths sum exactly to the declared SEQUENCE length. If an element claims a length larger than the remaining SEQUENCE content, `length` becomes negative and the method returns without error, accepting malformed DER. Also, after finishing the loop it does not check whether there are trailing bytes left in the underlying input beyond the SEQUENCE content. Additionally, readLength() only does an out-of-bounds check for long-form lengths (`length > 127`); short-form lengths skip any `limit`-based bounds validation, relying on EOF during read() instead of rejecting inconsistent encodings early.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:69 — Ignored providers are logged by passing a concatenated non-constant string as the debugf format, which builds the string even when debug is off and leaves a trailing ", "

adjudication.rationale: In CryptoIntegration.detectProvider, when multiple providers are found it builds a StringBuilder and then calls `logger.debugf(builder.toString());`. This eagerly constructs the full message regardless of whether debug logging is enabled (no `isDebugEnabled()` guard / supplier), and the loop appends `", "` after every provider, leaving a trailing comma+space in the logged message. This is a real, diff-grounded logging/perf/formatting issue but not a functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Removing the fail-closed "multiple providers" error while FIPS1402Provider, DefaultCryptoProvider and WildFlyElytronProvider all return order 200 means ServiceLoader/classpath order silently picks the winner (logged only at debug), so an auto-detecting FIPS deployment with the default jar also present can downgrade to non-FIPS BouncyCastle

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider() to no longer fail when multiple CryptoProvider implementations are found; it now sorts by CryptoProvider::order (descending) and returns the first provider, merely logging the rest at debug. However, DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return the same order value (200) in this diff, so the "winner" among them is determined by ServiceLoader iteration/classpath order when orders tie. That makes provider selection potentially non-deterministic and can select a non-FIPS provider even when a FIPS provider is present, whereas previously the code would throw on multiple providers.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:109 — concatenatedRSToASN1DER (the verify path for attacker-supplied JWS signatures) never checks signature.length == signLength, so extra trailing bytes are silently ignored (malleable signatures still verify) and short input throws an unchecked ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of IOException

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the method copies exactly `len` bytes for R and S from `signature` via `System.arraycopy(signature, 0, r, 1, len)` and `System.arraycopy(signature, len, s, 1, len)` with no validation that `signature.length == signLength`. If `signature.length < signLength`, `arraycopy` will throw an unchecked `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` rather than an `IOException`. If `signature.length > signLength`, trailing bytes are ignored (only the first `signLength` bytes are used), meaning distinct inputs can map to the same DER signature, which is a correctness/security concern in signature verification contexts.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:49 — The hand-rolled DER decoder is lenient: it ignores tag class/constructed bits, does not enforce that the SEQUENCE length matches its contents or reject trailing data, accepts non-minimal/negative INTEGERs, and throws an unchecked NumberFormatException on a zero-length INTEGER, all of which combine with integerToBytes (line 151) silently truncating oversized or negative r/s instead of rejecting them

adjudication.rationale: The new ASN1Decoder/ASN1Encoder + ECDSA conversion code is indeed permissive in the ways described. In ASN1Decoder.readSequence(), the tag check uses readTagNumber(tag) (masking with 0x1f) and does not validate the tag class/constructed bits, so any tag with low bits == 0x10 passes. The sequence length accounting (`while (length > 0) { bytes = readNext(); length -= bytes.length; }`) does not enforce exact consumption: if an element TLV exceeds the remaining declared length, `length` can go negative and the loop exits without error, and it also never checks for trailing data after the sequence. In readInteger(), a zero length leads to `new BigInteger(new byte[0])`, which throws an unchecked NumberFormatException. Integers are parsed with `new BigInteger(bytes)` allowing negative/non-canonical encodings. Finally, AuthzClientCryptoProvider.integerToBytes truncates when `qLength < bytes.length` by taking the last qLength bytes, silently accepting oversized (or negative) r/s values instead of rejecting them. These behaviors are all visible in the diff and can lead to incorrect/unsafe DER handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:42 — A single default-curve EC key is reused for ES256/ES384/ES512, so the P-384 and P-521 paths (66-byte odd r/s, long-form DER length >127) are never exercised; padding/truncation hides the curve mismatch and the tests pass anyway.

adjudication.rationale: The test creates a single EC keypair once in the constructor via `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` and reuses it for ES256/ES384/ES512 (see `ECDSAAlgorithmTest` lines ~33-69). The curve is not selected per algorithm, so ES384/ES512 may still be signing with the default EC parameters (commonly P-256). The conversion code then pads/truncates to `algorithm.getSignatureLength()` in `asn1derToConcatenatedRS`/`integerToBytes`, so the round-trip can pass even if the underlying key curve doesn’t match the algorithm’s expected signature size, meaning P-384/P-521-specific DER/length edge cases aren’t actually exercised by these tests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:56 — The round-trip assertion only compares the provider's own output with itself; it never checks the re-encoded DER against the original JDK signature or runs Signature.verify, so a bug that is symmetric in both directions would still pass.

adjudication.rationale: In ECDSAAlgorithmTest.test(...), the only assertion is Assert.assertArrayEquals(rsConcat, rsConcat2) after doing provider-based DER→RS and RS→DER conversions and back again. It never compares the provider-produced DER (asn1Des) to the original JDK Signature output (sign), nor does it perform Signature.verify on either form. Therefore a symmetric encode/decode bug in AuthzClientCryptoProvider’s ECDSA conversions could still pass this round-trip test, making the finding valid as a test completeness issue rather than a functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:134 — ASN1Decoder/ASN1Encoder have no direct tests and nothing covers malformed DER (wrong tag, sequence size != 2, truncated input, indefinite length -1 causing NegativeArraySizeException in read), long-form lengths, or high-tag-number parsing.

adjudication.rationale: ASN1Decoder.readLength() explicitly returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding (0x80). That value is then used unchecked as an array size in read(int length) (e.g., readInteger(): `int length = readLength(); byte[] bytes = read(length);`), which would trigger a NegativeArraySizeException rather than a controlled IOException. This is a real, diff-introduced correctness/robustness defect in the new ASN1Decoder, and the new ECDSAAlgorithmTest only covers happy-path roundtrips, not malformed DER inputs.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — The behavior change from throwing on multiple providers to sorting by order() has no test for multi-provider selection or for ties (Default/Elytron/FIPS all return 200, so the pick depends on ServiceLoader order).

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` to allow multiple `CryptoProvider`s and select one by sorting `order()` descending (`.sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())`) instead of throwing when `foundProviders.size() > 1`. However, no tests are added for this new selection behavior (only an ECDSA conversion test is added), and the diff shows `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`, and `FIPS1402Provider` all return the same `order()` value (200), meaning ties will be resolved by `ServiceLoader` iteration order, which is not asserted or made deterministic in the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/AuthzClient.java:95 — The test creates AuthzClientCryptoProvider directly, so no test checks the META-INF/services registration or that AuthzClient.create() initializes CryptoIntegration with the expected provider.

adjudication.rationale: The added test `ECDSAAlgorithmTest` directly instantiates `new AuthzClientCryptoProvider()` and exercises only the ECDSA conversion logic. It does not verify the SPI registration added at `authz/client/src/main/resources/META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider` is actually discoverable via `ServiceLoader`, nor does it cover the new initialization path `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())` added in `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)`. This is a specific, diff-grounded gap in test coverage for the newly introduced provider-discovery/initialization wiring, not a runtime defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:46 — High-bit and short (leading-zero) r/s only get covered by chance from one random signature per run, with no deterministic vectors, so integerToBytes padding and sign-byte handling are not reliably tested.

adjudication.rationale: The new test `ECDSAAlgorithmTest` generates a random EC keypair and performs a single sign/convert/convert-back roundtrip per algorithm (`testES256/384/512`). That means edge cases in `AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider()`—notably `integerToBytes()` truncation/left-padding behavior and BigInteger sign/leading-zero handling when DER integers have the high bit set—are only exercised if they happen to occur in that one random signature. The diff contains no deterministic vectors or targeted cases to reliably cover those conditions, so the finding is a valid, diff-grounded test coverage concern rather than a product defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/pom.xml:67 — The hamcrest test dependency is added but no test uses it (ECDSAAlgorithmTest only uses org.junit.Assert).

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new test-scoped dependency on `org.hamcrest:hamcrest` in `authz/client/pom.xml`, but the only newly added test (`authz/client/src/test/java/.../ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java`) imports and uses `org.junit.Assert` and has no Hamcrest imports/usages. From the diff alone, Hamcrest appears unused (though other pre-existing tests not shown could still rely on it).
